text:
Auction Bingo · 7 main contestants and guest G01 · 7 rounds

1. Preparation
Everyone receives the same 3×3 bingo board, 7 name tickets, and three 1-won coins, three 2-won coins, two 3-won coins, one 5-won coin, and one 10-won coin (30 won in total). From top to bottom, the bingo board is [triangle, circle, triangle] / [circle, star, circle] / [star, circle, triangle]. Coins cannot be broken into smaller denominations or transferred to anyone else.

2. Shape Selection and Bidding
Each round, shape selection is followed by private bidding. Each player chooses one of triangle, circle, or star, and everyone's chosen shape is revealed after all players have chosen. Players combine their available coins to bid at least 1 won on their chosen shape. When bidding, a player may exchange 1 Piece for one 1-won coin. The exchanged coin may be used in the bid or kept, and the exchanged Piece is not returned. Coins used in a bid are spent regardless of whether the player wins an auction. Anyone unable to pay at least 1 won in any round is automatically ranked last.

3. Winning an Auction and Private Information
The highest bidder for each shape receives as many copies of that shape as the number of players who selected it. If the highest bids are tied, that shape is divided equally among the tied bidders, and any remainder is discarded. Neither who won an auction nor the number of shapes obtained is disclosed, even to the winners themselves. Public announcements show only the winning price for each shape. All shapes whose winning price is the highest among the three shapes are marked Secret. If multiple shapes tie for the highest winning price, all of them are hidden. A shape that no one selected is marked as having no auction.

4. Final Results
After 7 rounds, the shapes obtained and the Secret winning prices are revealed. Individual bid amounts remain private. Excess shapes are discarded, and the shapes are automatically placed to maximize the number of bingo lines. Rankings are determined by comparing, in order, the number of completed horizontal, vertical, and diagonal lines, the number of filled squares, and the total value of remaining coins. Excluding the guest, the top 2 players go to Living Quarters, the next 4 go to Prison Wing, and the bottom 1 is eliminated. The first-place main contestant uses an Alliance Token to move one person from Prison Wing to Living Quarters. Anyone who fills all 9 squares receives 4 Pieces. The guest is excluded from Living Quarters, Prison Wing, and elimination determinations, and there is a prize of 10 million won each for placing first overall and completing the bingo board.

5. Simulator Progression Rules
After the rules are revealed and before the first conversation, refine the private strategy summary in 3 stages. Before the game begins, each participant has 10 conversation turns. Each round, conversations before shape selection and after the selections are revealed but before bidding each have a maximum of 6 turns. Each round's conversation ends when everyone passes, while still observing the minimum number of conversation turns before bidding. Players may use conversations with everyone, discussion room movement, invitations, and conversations, and 1:1 or group whispers among people in the same location. Update the private strategy summary immediately before bidding. After each conversation segment and public announcement, privately review affinity and trust based on new evidence. Complete ties and the order among multiple automatically last-ranked players are resolved using the default order drawn at the start. The guest also competes to accomplish their own two missions and has no obligation to cooperate with other participants.

6. Free Submission
For both shape selection and bidding, players may privately submit a final decision on their own turn when submissions are permitted during the respective conversation period of up to 6 turns. Once submitted, it cannot be changed or submitted again. Players who have submitted may still talk or move while other participants decide. The publicly displayed submission status shows only which participants have completed their submissions, without showing their shapes or bid amounts. Once everyone has submitted, that stage ends immediately without any remaining conversation. When 6 turns have ended, or when everyone passes after the minimum conversation turns have been completed, only those who have not submitted make their final submissions. Shapes are revealed together after everyone has submitted, and individual bid amounts remain private. Organize the pre-bid strategy summary before beginning the bidding conversation, and update strategy notes on every turn during the conversation. Coins used and Pieces exchanged are settled as soon as the bid is finalized.

7. Bidding in the Dealer Room
Upon finalizing a bid, visit the dealer room on the right to submit it privately, then immediately return to the hallway. Anyone who was in a discussion room is also located in the hallway after bidding, so subsequent whispers and discussion room conversations are based on the updated locations. Players cannot converse or remain inside the dealer room.

8. Minimum Conversation Before Bidding
After shape selections are revealed and before bidding, each participant has at least 3 turns of conversation. Bids cannot be submitted on turns 1–3, and play continues until the minimum conversation turns have been completed even if everyone passes. Starting on turn 4, participants can finalize their bids on their own turns. If everyone passes after the minimum conversation turns have been completed, the conversation ends and those who have not yet submitted bids submit them. This restriction does not apply to conversation before shape selection, so shapes can be submitted starting on the first turn.

fields.note: P06 is 3rd in the main competition's default tie-breaking order, so they need to secure a bingo rather than rely on a scoreless tie. A Piece exchange should be considered only when funds are insufficient or competition is decisive.

P05 plans based on the number of shapes needed for completion and the funds needed for minimum bids over 7 rounds. Since auction wins are private, they do not treat estimated acquisitions as confirmed.
P15 needs 3 triangles, 4 circles, and 2 stars for completion and considers both overspending and acquiring duplicates risky because auction-win information is hidden.

P04 is last in the default order, so they must avoid a complete tie. Since auction wins cannot be known, allowing a margin in estimated acquisitions and preventing funds from running out is more favorable for survival.

P07 secures shapes in a balanced way to avoid elimination, while prioritizing combinations used in multiple bingo lines. Since auction wins are unconfirmed, they distinguish estimates from confirmed information.

P14 is lowest among the main-competition players in the default order, so they must avoid a complete tie. Since auction wins are unconfirmed, they distinguish expected acquisitions from confirmed information.
G01 is excluded from elimination decisions, so they prioritize 1st place overall and the completion prize, valuing the number of bingo lines and filled squares more than the remaining balance.

P06 aims for completion with 3 triangles, 4 circles, and 2 stars, but first secures the right-hand vertical line with 3 triangles, then adds lines with circles and stars. Of the 30 won, they must reserve at least 1 won for each subsequent round. Depending on the number of selectors and the competition, they compare concentrated bidding with low-price acquisitions, recording auction wins as possible ranges rather than confirmed outcomes. After securing 1 line for survival, they aim for the top 2 in the Living Quarters and completion, using a Piece exchange only when it is decisive.

P05 aims for completion with 3 triangles, 4 circles, and 2 stars, but first secures the 2 central horizontal and vertical lines with 1 triangle, 2 circles, and 1 star, targeting survival and a top-2 finish. Each time, they preserve at least 1 won for each remaining round and the actual coin combinations needed, concentrating on shapes with weaker competition relative to the number of selectors. Using the public price and their own bid, they classify acquisitions as possible, uncertain, or failed. For cooperation, they propose avoiding competition by shape, but do not treat promises as auction wins. They consider a Piece exchange only when funds are insufficient.

P15 prioritizes avoiding elimination and aims for at least 2 lines and the top 2 in the Living Quarters. The completion target is 3 triangles, 4 circles, and 2 stars. Each time, they secure coins for minimum bids in the remaining rounds and concentrate on needed shapes based on the number of selectors and the competition. With 2 stars and 1 circle, the central vertical line is possible. They classify auction wins as confirmed, possible, or unknown, and reduce additional spending on shapes they are likely to have acquired in sufficient quantities. They consider a Piece exchange only when necessary for survival or a decisive auction win, and check the conditions under which protection promises will be carried out.

P04 aims for completion with 3 triangles, 4 circles, and 2 stars, but first secures shapes that will form multiple lines to avoid elimination and target the top 2. Each time, they retain a coin combination that allows a bid of at least 1 won in each remaining round. They concentrate on shapes with weaker competition relative to the number of selectors and use 10 won on an opportunity to acquire a large quantity. They estimate the possible range of acquisitions from the winning price and their own bid, accounting for distribution in ties and rounding down. They do not count cooperation promises as confirmed acquisitions, and use a Piece exchange only when necessary for survival or a decisive auction win.

P07 aims for completion with 3 triangles, 4 circles, and 2 stars, but first targets the two lines possible with 1 triangle, 1 circle, and 1 star, and the diagonal with 2 triangles and 1 star. They retain coins for a minimum bid each round and concentrate funds on auctions with many selectors where they can obtain the needed quantity in one go. They estimate the range of acquisitions from the public winning price and their own bid, maintaining two scoring paths. After securing survival, they aim for the Living Quarters and victory, considering a Piece exchange only when necessary for minimum bids or decisive competition.

P13 aims to complete 9 squares and 8 lines with 3 triangles, 4 circles, and 2 stars, but first secures the 1 diagonal line possible with 2 triangles and 2 circles, then adds stars to increase the number of lines. Of the 30 won, they preserve a coin combination that allows a bid of at least 1 won in each remaining round. They concentrate bids on needed shapes based on the number of selectors and the competition, and do not confirm acquisitions from the public winning price alone. They evaluate cooperation by distinguishing proposals from follow-through, and use a Piece exchange only when it materially improves the chances of survival or completion.

P14 aims for completion with 3 triangles, 4 circles, and 2 stars, but first targets 2 bingos—the top row and the central vertical line—with 2 triangles, 2 circles, and 1 star. Each time, they secure the minimum bids for the remaining rounds through actual coin combinations, concentrating spending on shapes with less competition relative to the number of selectors. They record the possible range of acquisitions using the public winning price and their own bid, accounting for distribution in ties and surplus shapes. They consider a Piece exchange when necessary to continue bidding or secure a decisive bingo. They prioritize survival while avoiding a complete tie.

G01 aims to complete 9 squares and 8 lines by securing 3 triangles, 4 circles, and 2 stars. Of the 30 won, they reserve the minimum bid amounts for subsequent rounds and concentrate on opportunities to obtain multiple shapes when there are many selectors. They manage both demand for circles and a shortage of stars, estimating auction wins from their bid amount and the public price rather than treating them as confirmed. They use a Piece exchange only to maintain minimum bids or for decisive competition.

Concentrating on triangles may result in only losing funds when there is competition, and auction wins cannot be confirmed through the end. Both the remaining amount and the coin composition must be checked to guarantee a minimum bid each round.

P05 confirmed that the shape quantities in the existing plan cannot create the central horizontal and vertical lines simultaneously. They revise their targets and fund management to account for uncertainty about private auction wins and coin consumption.

They corrected the requirement for the central vertical line to 2 circles and 1 star. They also account for uncertainty about auction wins and the number of coins to prevent being unable to bid in later rounds.

P04 is last in the default order and is therefore disadvantaged in a complete tie. P04 does not overestimate uncertain acquisition quantities and separately considers securing a line for survival and challenging for a high ranking.

P07 loses funds even when failing to win an auction, and the quantity secured decreases in a tie, so P07 does not treat estimated quantities as certain. P07 is second in the default order and is therefore advantaged in a complete tie.
P13 corrects the previous diagonal calculation and first secures funds for survival, accounting for uncertainty in winning auctions and coin expenditure.
P14 accumulates expenses even when failing to win an auction and is disadvantaged in a complete tie, so P14 prioritizes verifiable acquisition opportunities while preserving funds for minimum bids.
G01 places importance on both the prospects of securing each shape and the capacity for subsequent bids, since even failing to win an auction incurs costs, rather than making one excessive bid.

P06 aims for 1 line by securing 3 triangles, but also compares the alternative of making diagonals with 2 stars and 2 triangles depending on the number of people selecting each shape and expected competition. Each time, P06 secures a combination of coins that allows a bid of at least 1 won in every remaining round. P06 concentrates bids when judging that many people have selected the shape and competition is low, and treats opponents' statements as assumptions. P06 records auction wins and acquisition quantities as possible ranges that account for distribution in ties, and retains failure scenarios as well. If completion remains possible, P06 prioritizes missing shapes but does not chase aggressively to make up for uncertain auction wins. P06 considers exchanging Piece only when it is decisive for maintaining minimum bids or improving rank.

P05 first aims for 1 line with 1 triangle, 2 circles, and 1 star. The 2 central horizontal and vertical lines require 4 circles and 1 star. P05 distinguishes acquisition quantities as certain, possible, or failed, and does not treat a Secret price as success. P05 adjusts the target shape based on the number of people selecting each shape and expected competition, and preserves an actual combination of coins that allows a bid of at least 1 won in every remaining round. With no competition, P05 bids 1 won; with competition, P05 bids according to the expected benefit of additional lines and cells. P05 verifies cooperation promises and considers exchanging Piece only to prevent automatic last place or secure a decisive line.

P15 prioritizes avoiding elimination while aiming for at least 2 lines and a top 2 ranking. The central vertical line requires 2 circles and 1 star, and the right vertical line requires 2 triangles and 1 circle. P15 secures enough individual coins to bid in every remaining round and determines bids based on competition relative to the number of people selecting the shape and the number of shapes needed. P15 estimates acquisition ranges from public winning prices and personal bids, but does not draw definite conclusions about Secret prices or ties. P15 avoids overspending early and acquiring duplicates, and focuses on missing shapes later. P15 uses Piece exchanges only when they have a substantial effect on continued bidding or improving rank, and distinguishes opponents' statements and promises of protection from actual submissions and results.

P04 preserves a combination of coins that allows a bid of at least 1 won in every remaining round. If the public winning price exceeds P04's own bid, P04 records a failure; if it is equal or Secret, P04 records a range of acquisition quantities. P04 compares possible bingo lines while accounting for distribution in ties, rounding down, and duplicate shapes. P04 uses 10 won when there is a high likelihood of obtaining multiple needed shapes, while also estimating competitors' remaining balances. P04 does not count statements of cooperation as guarantees. Since a complete tie is disadvantageous, P04 aims for additional lines after securing the survival threshold, and limits Piece exchanges to decisive bids or maintaining minimum bids.

P07 preserves a combination of coins sufficient for minimum bids in every remaining round. Even a bid matching the public highest price leaves open the possibility of a tie, so P07 records lower and upper bounds for the quantity of each shape secured. P07 first aims for the two lines requiring 1 of each of the three shapes, while keeping diagonals requiring 2 triangles and 1 star or 1 triangle and 2 stars as alternatives. P07 concentrates bids by comparing the number of people selecting each shape with the quantity needed, and reduces spending on excess shapes. For cooperation, P07 trusts only verifiable coordination of selections, and later evaluates elimination risk using conservatively estimated quantities secured and competitors' possible numbers of lines. P07 limits Piece exchanges to maintaining minimum bids or opportunities to change rank.

P13 accounts for diagonals requiring 2 triangles and 1 star or 1 triangle and 2 stars. After every bid, P13 preserves an actual combination of coins that allows a bid in every remaining round. P13 concentrates bids based on the number of shapes needed relative to the number of people selecting them and the competition, while calculating full expenditure upon failure and distribution in ties. P13 does not confirm acquisitions based only on public prices and statements, and compares subsequent choices for each possible holding quantity. P13 first secures 1 line and filled cells, then aims for additional lines and completion of all 9 cells. P13 considers exchanging Piece when necessary to maintain minimum bids or compete for key shapes.

Before every bid, P14 sets aside an actual combination of coins that allows a bid of at least 1 won in every remaining round. If P14 is the sole person selecting a shape, P14 secures 1 shape for 1 won; when there is competition, P14 sets a spending cap accounting for the number of people and distribution in ties. P14 prioritizes 2 bingos with 2 triangles, 2 circles, and 1 star, but records acquisition quantities separately as certain quantities and possible ranges. P14 does not conclude that an auction was won based only on Secret prices and opponents' statements. If competition overheats, P14 switches to securing other shapes and increasing the number of filled cells, and exchanges Piece only when there is a substantial prospect of continued bidding or improved rank.

G01 aims for completion and 1st place overall with 3 triangles, 4 circles, and 2 stars. G01 does not assume auction wins and estimates ranges of quantities secured from public prices and personal bid amounts. G01 chooses which competitions to enter based on the number of people selecting each shape, missing shapes, and opponents' remaining budgets, and also takes advantage of low-cost acquisitions as the sole person selecting a shape. G01 accounts for distribution in ties and waste from excess shapes, and preserves an actual combination of coins that allows a bid in every remaining round.
